marble.name: Statistical questions
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.description: Distinguish a statistical question — one that anticipates variability in the data collected to answer it, so its answer must account for that variability (even when it is reported as a single summary value such as a mean or median) — from a question answered by a single fixed fact; for a statistical question, identify
marble.prompt: If you ask you whether 'How many pets does our family have?' and 'How many pets do children in your class have?' are the same kind of question, can they explain that the second one has lots of different answers — so you'd need to collect data from many people — while the first has just one answer?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning to organise and count information by sorting objects into groups and comparing which groups have more or fewer items.

misconceptions: 'Any question about lots of people is statistical.'
authoredAnswer: The registration count is one fixed current fact; journey times anticipate variable observations. Population is the specified pupils; attribute is journey duration with a defined method/unit. Median journey time remains statistical because it summarizes those variable data.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Calls a fixed group membership count statistical without identifying varying response data. Source basis: Bargagliotti et al. (2020), Pre-K–12 GAISE II, Framework and Levels A/B; official ASA report. The child-voice word
wrongAnswers.fix: Contrast group size with a variable measured for each member and identify the actual observations.

before.name: Sorting into categories (age 6+)
before.reason: Experience asking and answering questions about collected categorical data gives the concrete basis for recognising which questions need data that varies

before.name: Statistical Analysis Vocabulary
before.reason: Terms such as data, sample and average help pupils describe the population, attribute and expected variation
